issues.legal_issue: A declaratory decree limiting an alienation to the alienor’s lifetime restores the property to the alienor’s estate at death, and heirs entitled under the succession law then in force may inherit it even if they could not have challenged the alienation under customary law.
material_facts: An ancestor sold ancestral property without legal necessity, and a competent reversioner obtained a declaratory decree that the sale would not bind the estate beyond the ancestor’s lifetime.
The ancestor died after the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 came into force, leaving sons, a widow, and daughters who inherited the estate under that Act.
The widow and daughters had been unable to contest the alienation under the customary law that applied when the earlier declaratory suit was brought.
issues.conclusion: The alienated property reverted to the ancestor’s estate on his death, and all persons entitled to inherit that estate under the Hindu Succession Act, including the widow and daughters, could claim their shares.
issues.legal_principle: A declaratory decree obtained by a competent reversioner does not make the alienation a nullity; it removes the obstacle to succession and restores the property to the alienor’s estate when the alienor dies. Where succession opens after the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 applies, Sections 2 and 4(1) govern devolution of the estate. A woman’s former inability under customary law to contest the alienation does not prevent her from inheriting under that Act. Section 6 of the Punjab Custom (Power to Contest) Act, 1920 restricted who could contest an alienation, but did not displace the statutory succession rights that arose when succession opened.

predicates.possession_claim_after_declaratory_decre: The claimants sought possession of property after an earlier declaratory decree concerning its alienation.
predicates.declaratory_decree_limited_alienation_to: A competent reversioner obtained a decree providing that the alienation would not bind the estate after the alienor’s lifetime.
predicates.alienor_died_after_succession_law_applie: The alienor died after the relevant succession law had come into force.
predicates.heirs_included_persons_entitled_under_th: The persons claiming the estate included heirs who were entitled to inherit under the succession law applicable when succession opened.

issues.definition: When a possession claim follows a decree limiting an alienation to the alienor’s lifetime and succession opens under a law entitling the claimants to inherit, those statutory heirs may claim the restored estate.

issues.legal_issue: An appellate court may grant the lawful shares of claimants who did not appeal or file objections when doing so is necessary to adjust the rights of all parties to the dispute.
material_facts: The sons, widow, and daughters jointly sued for possession of the entire property from the alienee’s successors.
The lower appellate court accepted the claim that the alienee had no continuing interest after the ancestor’s death but granted possession only to the sons.
The widow and daughters did not appeal or file cross-objections, and the alienee’s successors appealed the decree.
issues.conclusion: The appellate court should exercise its power to grant the widow and daughters their lawful shares despite their not having appealed or filed cross-objections.
issues.legal_principle: Order 41, Rule 33 of the Code of Civil Procedure empowers an appellate court to pass a decree that ought in law to have been passed, including in favour of a party who did not appeal or object. Where the appellate court rejects the opposing party’s claim to retain the property, it may adjust the rights of the other parties to ensure that the decree accords with their legal entitlements.

predicates.appeal_in_joint_possession_suit: An appeal arose from a suit in which multiple claimants jointly sought possession of property.
predicates.joint_claimants_sought_the_entire_proper: The claimants’ joint suit sought possession of the entire disputed property.
predicates.appellate_court_found_alienee_had_no_con: The appellate court accepted that the alienee had no continuing interest in the property after the relevant owner’s death.
predicates.some_claimants_did_not_appeal_or_object: Some parties seeking shares in the property neither appealed nor filed objections to the decree.

issues.definition: When an appeal in a joint possession suit establishes that the opposing party has no continuing interest, the appellate court may grant lawful shares to claimants who did not appeal or object.

issues.legal_issue: A party may not reopen a part of a decree that was not challenged by appeal.
material_facts: The High Court decreed a share of the property in favour of the sons.
The respondents did not appeal against that part of the High Court’s decree.
issues.conclusion: The respondents could not challenge the decree granting the sons their share in the appeal before the Court.
issues.legal_principle: A party cannot use an appeal to challenge a part of the decree that has not been appealed against by that party and is not otherwise under challenge in the appeal.

predicates.appeal_from_decree: An appeal was brought from a decree.
predicates.decree_granted_relief_to_a_party: The decree granted relief to a party.
predicates.opposing_party_did_not_appeal_that_part: The opposing party did not appeal the part of the decree granting that relief.

issues.definition: In an appeal from a decree, relief granted in a part that the opposing party did not appeal cannot be reopened at that party’s instance.

issues.legal_issue: The Hindu Succession Act, 1956 does not retrospectively enlarge the alienor’s power over ancestral property or nullify a declaratory decree made before the Act came into force.
material_facts: The ancestor had alienated ancestral property and a declaratory decree had been made concerning that alienation before the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 came into force.
The respondents argued that the Act made the ancestor a full owner and left his sons without a subsisting reversionary interest despite the earlier decree.
issues.conclusion: The Act did not retrospectively enlarge the ancestor’s power over the ancestral property or nullify the earlier declaratory decree.
issues.legal_principle: Nothing in the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 operates retrospectively to enlarge the power of a holder of ancestral land or to nullify a declaratory decree passed before the Act came into force.

predicates.appeal_in_property_dispute: An appeal concerned rights to property.
predicates.ancestral_property_was_alienated_before_: An ancestor alienated ancestral property before the relevant succession law came into force.
predicates.declaratory_decree_preceded_succession_l: A declaratory decree concerning the alienation was made before the relevant succession law came into force.
predicates.retrospective_effect_is_claimed: A party claimed that the later succession law retrospectively changed the effect of the prior alienation or decree.

issues.definition: When ancestral property was alienated and a declaratory decree was made before a later succession law, a claim of retrospective effect does not displace that decree.
